lessons.0.slides.0.subtitle: Lesson 1 - 18 minutes
lessons.0.slides.0.description: Understand why vintage matters so much in Burgundy
lessons.0.slides.1.title: Why Are Vintages So Important?
lessons.0.slides.1.content: Burgundy sits at the northern limit of viticulture (47° north latitude), making climate swings profoundly influential on ripeness. The same plot from the same producer can produce wines that differ wildly in quality between years — and in price by a factor of 3–5.
lessons.0.slides.2.title: 🌤️ Vintage-Influencing Factors
lessons.0.slides.2.points.0: Spring frost — determines yield (severe frost can reduce crop by 50–90%)
lessons.0.slides.2.points.1: Summer temperatures — influence ripeness and style
lessons.0.slides.2.points.2: September weather — determines harvest timing and quality
lessons.0.slides.2.points.3: Rainfall — affects concentration and vine health
lessons.0.slides.2.points.5: Diurnal temperature swings — affect acidity and aromatics
lessons.0.slides.3.title: 📅 Vintage Classification Standards
lessons.0.slides.3.points.0: Great — perfect conditions, once in a generation
lessons.0.slides.3.points.3: Average — mixed results, must choose carefully
lessons.0.slides.3.points.5: Top producers make fine wine in any vintage
lessons.0.slides.4.title: Good Vintage vs. Poor Vintage
lessons.0.slides.5.title: Cool Vintage vs. Hot Vintage
lessons.0.slides.6.title: Vintage vs. Terroir vs. Producer
lessons.0.slides.6.content: Importance ranking: Producer > Terroir > Vintage. A top producer's Grand Cru in a difficult vintage still outperforms an ordinary producer's village wine in a great vintage. But in truly great vintages, even average producers can make excellent wine.

lessons.1.slides.0.subtitle: Lesson 2 - 22 minutes
lessons.1.slides.0.description: In-depth analysis of the pivotal vintages from 2000 to 2020
lessons.1.slides.1.title: 🏆 Great Vintages
lessons.1.slides.1.points.1: Outstanding red and white, extreme concentration, 30–50-year ageing potential
lessons.1.slides.1.points.3: Warm year, full-bodied wines, particularly excellent reds
lessons.1.slides.1.points.5: Cool year, elegant balance, especially fine for whites
lessons.1.slides.1.points.7: Warm but balanced, excellent for both reds and whites
lessons.1.slides.1.points.9: Moderately warm, good acidity, exceptional ageing potential
lessons.1.slides.2.title: ✅ Excellent Vintages
lessons.1.slides.2.points.0: 2002 — elegant and refined, now entering its drinking window
lessons.1.slides.2.points.1: 2012 — low yield, high quality; an underrated vintage
lessons.1.slides.2.points.3: 2017 — frost reduced yields but quality is excellent
lessons.1.slides.2.points.4: 2018 — warm year, rich and generous fruit
lessons.1.slides.3.title: ⚠️ Vintages Requiring Careful Selection
lessons.1.slides.3.points.0: 2003 — excessive heat, lost balance (select very carefully)
lessons.1.slides.3.points.1: 2004 — mixed results, must choose top producers
lessons.1.slides.3.points.3: 2007 — difficult vintage, not recommended for investment
lessons.1.slides.3.points.4: 2008 — cool year, whites better than reds
lessons.1.slides.3.points.5: 2011 — early-ripening vintage, mostly drinking well now
lessons.1.slides.4.title: Vintage Buying Strategy
lessons.1.slides.4.content: For investment and cellaring: choose great vintages such as 2005, 2009, 2010, 2015, 2019. For everyday drinking: excellent vintages like 2014, 2017, 2018 offer superior value. Avoid: difficult vintages like 2003, 2007, and 2013 — unless from a top producer.

lessons.2.title: The Impact of Climate Change
lessons.2.slides.0.title: Climate Change Impact
lessons.2.slides.0.subtitle: Lesson 3 - 20 minutes
lessons.2.slides.0.description: Explore the effects of global warming on Burgundy
lessons.2.slides.1.title: The Facts of Rising Temperatures
lessons.2.slides.1.content: Over the past 30 years, average temperatures in Burgundy have risen by approximately 1.5 °C. Harvest has moved forward by 2–3 weeks. In the 1980s the average harvest date was late September; today it is early September. This brings both opportunity and challenge.
lessons.2.slides.2.title: ✅ Positive Impacts
lessons.2.slides.2.points.0: Grapes ripen more easily, reducing under-ripe vintages
lessons.2.slides.2.points.1: More moderate acidity — not excessively high
lessons.2.slides.2.points.2: Natural alcohol of 12.5–13.5% achieved more reliably
lessons.2.slides.3.title: ⚠️ Negative Impacts
lessons.2.slides.3.points.2: Alcohol levels too high — loss of elegance
lessons.2.slides.3.points.3: More frequent extreme weather — frost, hail, drought
lessons.2.slides.3.points.4: Increased pests and diseases — more intervention needed
lessons.2.slides.3.points.5: Traditional style at risk — Burgundy's defining character threatened
lessons.2.slides.4.title: Growers' Adaptation Strategies
lessons.2.slides.4.content: Adjusting harvest timing (harvesting earlier to preserve acidity), changing viticultural practices (more shade, less leaf removal), selecting different rootstocks, adjusting fermentation temperatures, reducing new oak usage, exploring higher-altitude sites.
lessons.2.slides.5.title: 🔮 Looking Ahead
lessons.2.slides.5.points.0: Will Burgundy come to resemble southern Burgundy/the Rhône?
lessons.2.slides.5.points.1: Higher-altitude sites (above 350 m) will gain importance
lessons.2.slides.5.points.2: Chablis may become the most stable appellation (cooler climate)
lessons.2.slides.5.points.3: The advantage of the Côte de Nuits may narrow
lessons.2.slides.5.points.4: Biodynamic and organic viticulture will grow in importance
lessons.2.slides.5.points.5: Preserving traditional Burgundy style will require active effort
lessons.2.slides.6.title: Investment Perspective
lessons.2.slides.6.content: Focus on producers adapting successfully to climate change. Invest in traditionally cool vintages (2010, 2014) as benchmarks of classic style. In recent vintages, favour wines that maintain acidity and elegance. Long-term, Chablis and other cool-climate appellations look increasingly attractive.
